chapter_title: Displaying On-Chain Data and Handling State in React

screens.title: Displaying On‑Chain Data and Handling State in React
screens.subtitle: Read program accounts, deserialize account buffers, and keep your UI in sync with Solana state.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on turning raw Solana account bytes into usable UI state and keeping that state fresh. You will learn how to fetch account data from a cluster, why Anchor’s program. account. fetch is the safest shortcut for deserialization, and how React hooks—useState and useEffect—connect those fetches to your interface. I will show a concrete example: a counter program whose current value is stored on-chain. We will derive the program-derived account, fetch and convert a BN into a JavaScript number, and update the displayed count after transactions. You will also learn to handle loading indicators and errors so users understand what is happening. Finally, you will see strategies for real-time updates, including subscribing to account changes and when to prefer re-fetching after transactions. By the end of this lesson you should be able to display on-chain data reliably and avoid common mistakes like stale UI, incorrect deserialization, and infinite re-renders. Think about a DApp you use: how would you show live balances without confusing the user? That is the practical aim here.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use Anchor's fetch to deserialize safely, connect fetches to React state with useEffect, and re-fetch after transactions or subscribe for real-time updates to avoid stale UI.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to fetch and deserialize custom program accounts from Solana, wire that data into React state, and present clear loading and error states. First, you'll learn to use @solana/web3. js to fetch raw account bytes and to understand what the AccountInfo buffer contains. Second, you will use Anchor's program. account. fetch A P I to convert that raw buffer into a typed JavaScript object, reducing manual deserialization effort. Third, you'll practice React patterns: useState to store fetched values and useEffect to trigger fetches when dependencies change. Fourth, you'll explore approaches for keeping the UI current: re-fetch after transactions, and subscribe with connection. onAccountChange for real-time updates when appropriate. Each objective includes a concrete reason why it matters: safe deserialization prevents subtle bugs, proper hooks prevent infinite re-renders, and clear loading UX avoids confusing users. A short example will show fetching a counter value and converting anchor. BN into a JavaScript number so the UI shows an accurate count.

narration.text: Successful implementation means your DApp not only fetches data correctly but also communicates state clearly to users. You should be able to present a loading flow when RPC calls are in flight and show friendly error messages if an account is missing or deserialization fails. You will practice disabling actions during pending transactions to prevent duplicate submissions. screens.title: What the AccountInfo buffer contains and why deserialize
screens.subtitle: Understanding raw account data and the role of deserialization

narration.text: On Solana every account exposed by the RPC returns an AccountInfo object that includes metadata and a data Buffer. That buffer is the serialized bytes representing the program-owned account state. Deserialization is the process of turning those bytes back into structured fields that your code can read, like a counter value stored as a u64. If you fetch raw AccountInfo directly, you must map bytes to types exactly as your on-chain program wrote them. This includes respecting byte order, sizes for integers, and layout for nested structs. Anchor simplifies that by generating an IDL that describes the account layout and by offering program. account. X. fetch which both fetches and deserializes according to the IDL. A concrete example: a counter account storing a u64 is returned as a Buffer. Using Anchor, fetch returns an object where count is an anchor. BN; you then convert that BN to a JavaScript number for display. A common misconception is that connection. getParsedAccountInfo will always produce typed fields; it often provides parsed data for native programs but not for your custom program accounts. The key takeaway: deserialize with the same layout used on-chain or use Anchor’s fetch to avoid subtle mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Deserialization core
keyIdea.text: The account data Buffer must be deserialized using the on-chain layout; Anchor's fetch uses the IDL to do this reliably.

content.html:
Definition AccountInfo Buffer
What is inside AccountInfo?
  • Owner, lamports, executable flag, and a data Buffer that contains serialized fields.
  • The Buffer follows the structure written by your program; fields must be parsed in the same order.
  • Deserialization turns bytes into usable primitives, arrays, or nested objects.
Concrete example
A Counter account contains a single u64. The Buffer holds eight bytes for that u64; Anchor returns an object with count as anchor.BN which you convert to number for display.
Anchor vs manual parsing
Use Anchor fetch to read and deserialize automatically according to the IDL.
Manual parsing requires exact byte offsets, integer widths, and endianness.
A common mistake: assuming parsed account formats apply to custom program accounts; they usually do not.

screens.title: Using Anchor's program.account.fetch in a component
screens.subtitle: A practical code example: fetch and convert a counter value

narration.text: Let's walk through the updated CounterProgramInteraction component and the key lines that fetch and display the count. The important pieces are: a memoized anchor. Program instance so we don't recreate the client, deriving the program-derived address for the counter using findProgramAddressSync, calling program. account. counterAccount. fetch(pda) to get a typed object, and converting account. count from anchor. BN to a JavaScript number with toNumber or toNumber() as shown. In practice you store the count in a useState variable and setLoading while the fetch runs. Remember to catch errors: an absent account or a deserialization mismatch will throw. After transactions that modify state, immediately call your fetch function again to update the UI. Concrete snippet in the lesson uses fetchCounter invoked from a useEffect whenever the counter PDA or program changes. A common misconception is to place fetch logic directly in render or to recreate the program instance on every render, which causes unnecessary RPC calls and may trigger infinite loops. The takeaway is to separate concerns: memoize the program, derive the PDA once, fetch in effects, and convert BN to safe numbers before rendering.

keyIdea.title: Code takeaway
keyIdea.text: Memoize program and fetch account with program.account.X.fetch then convert anchor.BN to a number and update React state safely.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Anchor fetch example
Key snippet (visual only)
// memoize program
const program = useMemo(() => {
  if (publicKey) {
    const provider = new anchor.AnchorProvider(connection, { publicKey, sendTransaction } as any, { commitment: 'confirmed' });
    return new anchor.Program(idl as anchor.Idl, programId, provider);
  }
  return null;
}, [connection, publicKey, sendTransaction]);

// fetchCounter
const account = await program.account.counterAccount.fetch(counterAccountPda);
setCurrentCount(account.count.toNumber());
Explanation cards
Memoize program to avoid reinitializing provider and repeating RPC setup.
Use program.account.X.fetch to both fetch and deserialize according to your IDL.
Convert BN to number before rendering; guard against overflow where needed.
Handle errors: if fetch fails reset state and show a helpful message.
Key Takeaway

Anchor fetch returns typed objects; convert anchor.BN to numbers and store in state to display safely.

screens.title: Deriving the Counter PDA and when to set it
screens.subtitle: A robust pattern for deriving and storing program-derived addresses

narration.text: A reliable DApp derives program-owned addresses deterministically so both the program and the client agree on locations. For our counter example, a common pattern is to derive the PDA from a seed like the string "counter" and the user's public key. Use PublicKey. findProgramAddressSync with the correct seeds and programId. In React you should compute the PDA only when you have the dependencies: a connected wallet publicKey and a ready anchor. Program instance. Memoize or wrap the derivation in a useCallback so you don't recompute it on every render. After wallet connection, set the PDA into state and trigger a fetch. If the wallet disconnects set PDA and currentCount back to null to avoid invalid fetch attempts. A frequent mistake is deriving PDAs before the program is available or using inconsistent seeds; this causes fetches to fail or to query the wrong account. Concrete example: derive once after connection, store it in useState, and useEffect will call fetchCounter when PDA changes. The learner takeaway: compute PDAs deterministically, guard on required dependencies, and avoid deriving inside render loops to prevent repeated RPC calls.

keyIdea.title: PDA pattern
keyIdea.text: Derive PDAs only when dependencies exist, memoize the derivation, and reset state on disconnect to prevent invalid fetches.

content.html:
Process Flow PDA derivation
Step-by-step
1. Wait for wallet connect
Ensure publicKey and program exist before deriving.
2. Derive PDA deterministically
Use PublicKey.findProgramAddressSync with the same seeds used on-chain.
3. Store PDA in state
Set counterAccountPda and trigger fetch via useEffect.
Visual code hint
const [counterPda, setCounterPda] = useState<PublicKey | null>(null);
useEffect(() => {
  if (connected && publicKey && program) {
    setCounterPda(getCounterPda());
  } else {
    setCounterPda(null);
    setCurrentCount(null);
  }
}, [connected, publicKey, program, getCounterPda]);
Avoid deriving inside render. Use useCallback or useMemo for getCounterPda to keep effects stable.

screens.title: Managing loading state and error messages
screens.subtitle: Clear UX patterns when fetching on-chain data

narration.text: Good UX around data fetching tells users what is happening and prevents harmful actions. In the counter component we use a loading state and a message string to communicate progress and errors. Before any fetch, setLoading(true) and setMessage('Fetching...') to show a spinner or an inline status. When the fetch succeeds setCurrentCount and setMessage('Counter fetched successfully.'). On errors, catch them, log for debugging, setCurrentCount(null), and setMessage with a readable summary. Also disable create and increment actions when loading so users cannot submit duplicate transactions. A concrete example: after calling program. methods. increment(). rpc() await confirmation, then call fetchCounter to update the UI and reset loading. Another important detail is to avoid infinite re-renders: do not use setState inside a render cycle and ensure fetch functions are stable via useCallback. A common mistake is clearing loading only on success; always clear it in finally so the UI does not stay stuck. The takeaway: explicit loading flags, descriptive messages, and disabling controls during RPC calls lead to predictable and safe UIs for your DApp. Managing loading state and error messages means set loading and message before rpc calls, clear loading in finally, and disable actions while requests pending to avoid duplicates.. In practical terms, clear ux patterns when fetching on-chain data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loading & error pattern
keyIdea.text: Set loading and message before RPC calls, clear loading in finally, and disable actions while requests pending to avoid duplicates.

content.html:
Process Loading & Error UX
Pattern
Before fetch
setLoading(true); setMessage('Fetching counter...')
On success
setCurrentCount(account.count.toNumber()); setMessage('Counter fetched successfully.')
On error
log error, setCurrentCount(null); setMessage('Error fetching counter: ...')
Finally
setLoading(false) so UI does not remain locked.
Concrete example
setLoading(true);
setMessage('Incrementing counter...');
try {
  await program.methods.increment().accounts({ counterAccount: counterPda, user: publicKey }).rpc();
  await fetchCounter();
  setMessage('Counter incremented successfully!');
} catch (err) {
  setMessage('Error incrementing: ' + err.message);
} finally {
  setLoading(false);
}
Always disable transaction controls while loading to prevent duplicate transactions and confusing state.

screens.title: Real-time updates: onAccountChange vs re-fetching
screens.subtitle: When to subscribe and when to re-fetch after transactions

narration.text: There are two pragmatic strategies for keeping your UI current: re-fetch after a transaction confirms and subscribe with connection. onAccountChange for real-time updates. Re-fetching is simple and efficient for actions initiated by your app: after you call rpc() and the transaction is confirmed, call fetchCounter to refresh the view. This avoids persistent subscriptions and conserves RPC quota. Subscriptions via connection. onAccountChange let you react instantly when any party updates the account, which is necessary for collaborative or multi-client scenarios. When using onAccountChange remember that each subscription consumes resources and public RPC endpoints may limit them. Also confirm that the callback re-fetches or deserializes correctly. A common misconception is thinking subscriptions always replace the need for re-fetching; in practice you may combine them: subscribe for push updates, but still re-fetch on transaction confirmation to ensure consistency. Concrete example: after incrementing, call fetchCounter; additionally, if you expect external changes, register a single onAccountChange listener for that PDA and update state from the returned buffer or call program. account. fetch. The takeaway: choose subscriptions when you need live pushes and accept their resource cost, otherwise prefer targeted re-fetches after transactions.

keyIdea.title: Update strategy
keyIdea.text: Re-fetch after your transactions for most flows; use onAccountChange for real-time multi-client updates, respecting RPC limits.

content.html:
Architecture Update strategies
Re-fetch after transaction
Call fetchCounter after rpc() confirmation. Best for actions initiated by this client and for conserving RPC usage.
Good for: single-user flows; low RPC cost
Subscribe with onAccountChange
Use connection.onAccountChange(publicKey, callback) to receive immediate notifications when account data changes.
Good for: collaborative apps, real-time feeds. Mind RPC quotas and cleanup of subscriptions.
Implementation note
Combine approaches: re-fetch after your own transactions and subscribe only if you need immediate external updates. Always remove subscriptions on cleanup to avoid leaks.

narration.text: You can parse account data manually or rely on Anchor's fetch. Manual deserialization gives you control and is necessary if you don't have an IDL, but it is error-prone. You must correctly interpret byte order, field sizes, alignment, and any nested structures. Even small mistakes lead to wrong values or runtime errors. Anchor's program. account. YourAccountName. fetch abstracts this: it fetches AccountInfo and deserializes according to the IDL produced at build time. This offers type safety and fewer bugs. The trade-off is that Anchor requires the IDL and its client; if you must support a minimal client or a non-Anchor program you need manual parsing. A concrete example: converting an eight-byte u64 into a number is straightforward with Anchor (you get anchor. BN), while manual parsing requires reading bytes and constructing the integer with the correct endianness. A common misconception is assuming parsed RPC responses always include typed fields for custom accounts; they usually do not. The takeaway: prefer Anchor fetch when building Anchor-based programs for reliability and faster implementation; use manual parsing only with care and test vectors. Manual deserialization vs Anchor's fetch means anchor fetch simplifies deserialization and reduces bugs; manual parsing is flexible but requires exact, tested layouts.. screens.title: React hooks required: useState, useEffect, useCallback
screens.subtitle: Patterns to manage fetched data and avoid infinite re-renders

narration.text: React hooks are how you connect fetched on-chain data to the visible UI. useState stores values like counterPda, currentCount, loading, and message. useEffect performs side effects such as calling fetchCounter when dependencies change. Without careful dependency lists, an effect can re-run repeatedly and cause infinite fetch loops or A P I-rate errors. To prevent that useCallback or useMemo for functions that appear in useEffect dependencies; this stabilizes function identity so effects run only when the underlying data changes. For example, wrap fetchCounter in useCallback with counterAccountPda and program as dependencies. Always guard effects: if the PDA or program is null, return early. A concrete scenario: when the wallet connects set the PDA, then useEffect detects a non-null PDA and calls fetchCounter once. A common misconception is to place fetch logic directly in render or to include objects with changing identity in the dependency array, triggering repeated fetches. The core habit is: stabilize functions and state, declare clear dependencies, and reset state when key inputs become invalid. React hooks required: useState, useEffect, useCallback means stabilize fetch functions with usecallback, guard effects with early returns, and reset state on disconnect to avoid invalid fetches.. In practical terms, patterns to manage fetched data and avoid infinite re-renders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hook patterns
keyIdea.text: Stabilize fetch functions with useCallback, guard effects with early returns, and reset state on disconnect to avoid invalid fetches.

content.html:
Definition React hooks pattern
Core hooks
useState to hold currentCount, loading, and PDA.
useEffect to trigger fetchCounter when PDA or program changes.
useCallback to memoize fetchCounter and PDA derivation functions.
Anti-patterns
- Putting fetch logic inside render.
- Using objects with changing identity in effect deps without memoizing.
- Forgetting to clear state when wallet disconnects.

screens.title: Common mistakes and production tips
screens.subtitle: Prevent stale UI, infinite re-renders, and RPC rate limits

narration.text: In production you must watch for a few recurring problems. First, stale UI: failing to call fetch after a transaction leaves users looking at old values. Fix this by calling your fetch function after rpc() completes. Second, infinite re-renders: using unstable functions or objects in useEffect dependencies can cause repeated fetch calls; solve this with useCallback or useMemo. Third, incorrect deserialization: manually parsing buffers without matching the on-chain layout leads to wrong values; prefer Anchor fetch or verified manual parsing using test vectors. Fourth, resource exhaustion: too many subscriptions or frequent polling can hit RPC rate limits. Use re-fetch-after-transaction for most cases and only open subscriptions for accounts that truly need live pushes. Another tip is to present helpful messages when an account is not found and suggest creating it. For example, if fetch throws because the account doesn't exist, prompt creation rather than showing an error stack. The takeaway: combine robust error handling, careful hook dependencies, and mindful RPC usage to make a resilient DApp. Common mistakes and production tips means re-fetch after transactions, memoize dependencies, prefer anchor fetch, and limit subscriptions to avoid rpc rate limits.. In practical terms, prevent stale ui, infinite re-renders, and rpc rate limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Production checklist
keyIdea.text: Re-fetch after transactions, memoize dependencies, prefer Anchor fetch, and limit subscriptions to avoid RPC rate limits.

content.html:
Best Practices Common mistakes
Stale UI
Always call fetch after a transaction completes so the UI reflects the new on-chain state.
Infinite re-renders
Memoize functions used in effects. Avoid changing dependencies each render.
RPC limits
Prefer targeted re-fetches and limit subscriptions to reduce RPC usage and rate limiting.
Pro tip
If fetch fails because an account is missing, show a guided prompt to create the account rather than a raw error message.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Three short concepts to carry away: First, Anchor's program. account. fetch is the most efficient, type-safe path to deserialize custom program accounts when you have an IDL. Second, useState and useEffect are the connective tissue between fetched on-chain values and your rendered UI; stabilize your fetches with useCallback and update after transactions to avoid stale displays. Third, choose your update strategy wisely: re-fetch after local transactions for simplicity and resource efficiency; subscribe with connection. onAccountChange only when you need push-style updates and can manage RPC usage and cleanup. Keep these three in mind while building: safe deserialization, stable React patterns, and mindful real-time updates. These small choices significantly improve correctness and user trust in your DApp. What to Remember means anchor fetch + react hooks + thoughtful update strategy = reliable, user-friendly on-chain data display.. narration.text: As you build, keep three short reminders: 1) prefer Anchor's fetch when you have an IDL — it reduces errors and returns typed objects; 2) stabilize your React effects and memoize program or fetch functions so you do not trigger repeated network requests; 3) balance accuracy and resources — re-fetch after your own transactions, and subscribe only when you need immediate external updates. Think of these as rules of thumb: safety-first for parsing, discipline for hooks, and pragmatism for updates. Apply them to the counter example and to any program account you display in the UI. Before you finish a feature, ask: does the UI show current state after actions? If not, add a targeted fetch or subscription with a clear cost assessment. That question keeps your DApp accurate and user-friendly.
